column6: Factoring out a GCF assumes students can find the GCF of the numerical coefficients.
The least common denominator is the LCM of the denominators.
Simplifying radicals presumes knowing which roots are rational and which are irrational.
The completeness axiom distinguishes ℝ from ℚ; the informal rational/irrational picture motivates it.
MAD is the first measure of spread around the mean; standard deviation refines it with squared deviations.
A linear function is a special case of the function concept defined here.
f(x) notation presupposes that each input has exactly one output.
Domain and range are introduced informally in the relations topic.
The two-tangent theorem in that topic is proved with HL (its own text says "hypotenuse-leg").
Similar right triangles explain why trigonometric ratios do not depend on triangle size.
Optimization on a closed interval uses the closed interval method.
The rigorous proof formalizes the Extreme Value Theorem first met here.
cos(iz) = cosh z and sin(iz) = i sinh z link the two families.
Hyperbolic substitutions are an alternative for integrals with √(x² + a²).
Graphs of functions of two variables are often quadric surfaces (paraboloids, saddles).
The Frobenius indicial equation generalizes the Cauchy-Euler indicial equation at a regular singular point.
Compactness of integral operators is usually proved with Arzelà-Ascoli.
The Peano existence theorem (continuous f only) is proved with Arzelà-Ascoli.
The implicit function theorem is derived from the inverse function theorem.
That topic invokes the inverse function theorem to show exp_p is a local diffeomorphism.
Classifying groups of order pq and similar uses semidirect products.
A Riemannian metric generalizes the first fundamental form from surfaces to manifolds.
The classical Gauss-Bonnet theorem is stated for surfaces with metric E, F, G.
Gauss-Bonnet integrates the Gaussian curvature.
Minimal surfaces are defined by mean curvature H = 0.
Sectional curvature generalizes the Gaussian curvature of a surface.
The Nullstellensatz motivates the ideal/variety correspondence behind Spec and the Zariski topology.
It links Krull dimension of affine algebras to geometric dimension.
Reflected Brownian motion arises as the heavy-traffic limit of queue lengths.
